RECAP.t: Nov 20 close: the S&P 500 fell 3.69% to 6,910.39, the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.28% to 22,617.73 and the Dow fell 1.93% to 48,147.33. The S&P 500 and Dow both confirmed corrections (down 10% or more from their highs).

CAL: The second estimate of Q3 growth plus the Fed's favorite inflation gauge, the day before Thanksgiving.
The Fed's December meeting decision, where markets are pricing a quarter-point hike.

NEWS.h: Nasdaq falls 5.28% and the S&P 500 and Dow confirm corrections as the AI selloff deepens
NEWS.w: Final closes Friday: the S&P 500 fell 3.69% to 6,910.39, the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.28% to 22,617.73 and the Dow fell 1.93% to 48,147.33. Reuters said Anthropic's debut fell flat and its shares posted a steep loss Friday. Fed Governor Lisa Cook said the policy rate is not high enough to deal with inflation levels, and CME FedWatch showed a near-certain quarter-point hike at the December meeting.
NEWS.m: A correction means an index is down at least 10% from its high. With rate hikes priced in and AI stocks falling together, valuations are being repriced across the market.
NEWS.a: Interview point: explain why higher rates hit long-duration growth stocks hardest (think of the discount rate in a DCF).

NEWS.h: US futures tick lower after the AI-driven selloff; Anthropic slips about 4% after hours
NEWS.w: Trading Economics reported US futures edged lower Friday after Anthropic's IPO. Anthropic shares fell nearly 4% in after-hours trading after a 17% gain on debut day. On Thursday all three major indexes fell more than 2%, with the Nasdaq Composite at its lowest since April. Nvidia fell 3.3% and AMD fell 7.7% after Hunterbrook Capital's short call.
NEWS.m: Investors are still testing how much AI optimism the market will pay for, and the new listing is trading with the tape.
NEWS.a: Interview point: explain how a short seller's report can move a stock and what a bank would check before responding.
s: Trading Economics, US stock market news (Nov 19-20)

NEWS.h: Stocks sink on Anthropic's debut day: Dow falls 2.19%, S&P 500 2.02%, Nasdaq 2.25%
NEWS.w: TradingKey reported closes of 49,097.06 for the Dow (-2.19%), 7,175.83 for the S&P 500 (-2.02%) and 23,879.20 for the Nasdaq Composite (-2.25%). The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 2.41% to 9,419.72, with 27 of 30 members lower. Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said AI data-center investment is pushing up inflation, per TradingKey.
NEWS.m: A record IPO did not stop a broad selloff, so rates and AI valuation worries are still setting the tone.
NEWS.a: Interview point: give two reasons a big IPO can pull money out of existing holdings in the same sector.

NEWS.h: Anthropic opens at $111.50 on its first day, then closes at $97.17, about 17% above the $83 IPO price
NEWS.w: Per TradingKey, Anthropic (ANT) opened about 34% above the $83 offer at $111.50, hit a high of $115.10, and closed at $97.17, about 17% above the IPO price. WSJ, as cited by TradingKey, put the market value slightly below $1.5 trillion at the open counting current shares, and above $2 trillion counting all potential future shares.
NEWS.m: An IPO pop shows buyers would pay more than the offer price, but a fade from the open shows how quickly early excitement cools.
NEWS.a: Interview point: explain what an IPO 'pop' means for the issuer (money left on the table).

NEWS.h: Intuit agrees to sell Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for $3.68 billion
NEWS.w: Panabee, summarizing the SEC filings, reported Bending Spoons will buy Mailchimp for $3.68 billion, subject to adjustments for cash, debt and working capital. Intuit will reinvest about $368 million (about 10% of the value) into newly issued Bending Spoons shares. Closing is expected in early 2027, and Intuit agreed not to compete with Mailchimp for two years after closing. Panabee notes its text is AI-generated and may contain numerical errors.
NEWS.m: Selling a non-core unit and taking part of the price in the buyer's stock keeps some upside while freeing cash.
NEWS.a: Interview point: explain why a seller might take part of the price in the buyer's shares.

NEWS.h: AMD falls 7.72% to $489.19 after a short seller alleges China exposure
NEWS.w: CNBC reported AMD closed down 7.72% at $489.19 after short seller Hunterbrook Media, which disclosed a short position, alleged that blacklisted Chinese server maker IEIT Systems kept receiving newer AMD firmware and that AMD bills over 20% of revenue to customers in China and Hong Kong. AMD said the claims misrepresent its business practices and that it complies with U.S. export controls. CNBC did not independently verify the allegations.
NEWS.m: A short seller profits if the stock falls, so its claims are a reason to dig in, not proof. Export-rule risk matters because it can cut off a big share of revenue.
NEWS.a: Interview point: explain why vendor financing raises revenue-quality questions.

NEWS.h: Anthropic prices IPO at $83 a share, above its range, raising about $81.3 billion in the largest listing on record
NEWS.w: Anthropic priced 980 million Class A shares at $83, above the marketed $70 to $78 range and up from 825 million shares originally planned. About 956.4 million shares come from the company and about 23.6 million from existing shareholders. The raise of roughly $81.3 billion tops the roughly $75 billion SpaceX raised in June, and the fully diluted valuation is about $1.5 trillion versus $965 billion privately in May (per PitchBook). Underwriters have a 30-day option for up to 147 million more shares (about $12.2 billion). Trading on Nasdaq under ANT was expected to begin Thursday, with the offering closing Friday.
NEWS.m: Pricing above the range and upsizing the deal shows demand beat supply, which is how bankers judge a successful book.
NEWS.a: Interview point: explain why a banker upsizes and prices above range, and what the greenshoe (overallotment option) does.

NEWS.h: Stocks slip as the Anthropic-debut rally fades; Dow drops below 50,000
NEWS.w: By 11:04 a.m. New York time Bloomberg showed the S&P 500 little changed, the Nasdaq 100 up 0.4% and the Dow down 0.8%. The 10-year Treasury yield was about 5.07%. WTI crude rose 1.2% to $84.23 and spot gold fell 1.3% to $3,678.55. The S&P 500 was heading toward its longest losing streak since April 2024. An analyst said the IPO is a major success but does not address AI profitability, heavy spending, higher rates or credit stress. A midmorning report put the VIX at 22.91. These are intraday numbers, not the close.
NEWS.m: Even a record IPO could not lift the whole market, so rates and AI valuation worries are still driving prices.
NEWS.a: Interview point: name two reasons a hot IPO might not lift the broader market (rates, concentration in AI names).

NEWS.h: Palo Alto beats and raises, and agrees to buy Applied Compute for $4.5 billion in stock
NEWS.w: Palo Alto Networks reported first-quarter revenue of $3.45 billion, up 39% and above the $3.31 billion LSEG estimate, and raised fiscal 2027 revenue guidance to $14.52 billion to $14.57 billion from $14.10 billion to $14.20 billion. It also agreed to buy AI startup Applied Compute for $4.5 billion, expected to close in the third quarter of fiscal 2027; reports describe the deal as all-stock. The shares were up about 5.7% midmorning Thursday after jumping in after-hours trading Wednesday.
NEWS.m: A cybersecurity leader is paying for an AI platform with its own stock, which keeps cash on hand.
NEWS.a: Interview point: explain why an acquirer might pay in stock instead of cash.

NEWS.h: Walmart raises its full-year outlook, but the stock is lower midmorning
NEWS.w: Bloomberg reported Walmart raised its full-year sales and earnings forecasts. A midmorning market report had the shares down about 1.1% despite the raise. Williams-Sonoma was down 8.6% on revenue just under forecasts. Intuit and Ross Stores report after the close.
NEWS.m: A raised forecast can still be met with a selloff if investors expected even more.
NEWS.a: Interview point: explain why a stock can fall after raising guidance (expectations already priced in).

NEWS.h: JPMorgan, Visa and Mastercard say some customer data was accessed in a vendor cyberattack
NEWS.w: Bloomberg reported JPMorgan Chase, Visa and Mastercard said some customer data was accessed in a cyberattack on a vendor. The same wrap noted AMD fell after Hunterbrook Capital said it was short the stock, and that SpaceX planned a debt sale of at least $32 billion tied to a chip-financing deal.
NEWS.m: Banks depend on third-party vendors, so a vendor breach becomes the bank's risk too.
NEWS.a: Interview point: name one risk of relying on third-party vendors (operational and data-security risk).

NEWS.h: Dow drops 561 points, S&P 500 slips for a fifth day, Nasdaq rises ahead of Anthropic IPO
NEWS.w: The S&P 500 closed at 7,323.63 (-0.23%), the Dow at 50,198.17 (-1.11%) and the Nasdaq at 24,429.88 (+0.42%). The Russell 2000 also rose. Nvidia closed at $150.96, down 2.89%, after reversing early gains even though fiscal Q3 revenue grew 103% year over year; it also halted about $2.4B in quarterly Hopper chip sales to China. Fed minutes showed nearly all policymakers saw more rate increases as likely, and October building permits fell 7.4%.
NEWS.m: The split between the Dow and Nasdaq shows investors rotating toward AI names while worrying about rates.
NEWS.a: Interview point: explain why the Nasdaq can rise while the Dow falls (different sector weights, and AI IPO excitement).

NEWS.h: Stocks slide again in late-morning trading even as Nvidia beats; Dow down about 1.3%
NEWS.w: Yahoo Finance's live page showed the S&P 500 at 7,297.48 (-0.59%), the Dow at 50,087.28 (-1.32%), the Nasdaq at 24,283.22 (-0.19%) and the Russell 2000 up 0.52%. The VIX was 24.89 and the 10-year Treasury yield 5.07%. Nvidia rose early but was down about 2.2% after trimming gains. Oil was around $83 and gold around $3,752.
NEWS.m: Good results from the biggest AI company did not lift the market, which suggests worries about rates and AI valuations matter more than one earnings report.
NEWS.a: Interview point: explain why a stock can fall after beating estimates (expectations were already priced in).

NEWS.h: Nvidia beats: $115.8B revenue vs about $108.8B expected, guides next quarter to $130B
NEWS.w: Nvidia reported fiscal Q3 revenue of $115.8 billion (forecast about $108.8B) and EPS of $2.68 (forecast $2.47), with a 74.9% gross margin and $107.6B of Data Center revenue. It guided Q4 revenue to $130 billion, plus or minus 3%, with gross margin of 71% to 72%. The stock rose more than 4% after hours.
NEWS.m: Beating by about $7B and guiding higher shows AI spending is still growing, though the stock had already fallen about 35% from its October high before the report.
NEWS.a: Interview point: know how analysts compare actual results to consensus and guidance.

NEWS.h: Target beats on sales and EPS, but shares trade lower premarket
NEWS.w: Target's Q3 net sales rose 7.1% to $27.1B (estimate $26.5B) and diluted EPS rose 49% to $2.65 (estimate $2.08), including a $0.50 benefit from tariff refunds. Shares were still moving lower premarket. Lowe's also beat estimates.
NEWS.m: A one-time benefit like tariff refunds inflates EPS, so analysts focus on adjusted or underlying results.
NEWS.a: Interview point: explain why you adjust for one-time items when valuing a company.

NEWS_QUIZ: Anthropic priced its IPO at $83, above the $70 to $78 range, and upsized the deal. What does that signal?
The company wanted a lower valuation
Underwriters could not sell the shares
Pricing above range and adding shares means investors wanted more stock than was offered.
Palo Alto is paying $4.5B for Applied Compute largely in its own stock. What is one reason to pay in stock?
It preserves cash and shares the risk with the target's holders
It is always cheaper than debt
It removes the need for shareholder value
Stock consideration keeps cash on hand but dilutes the acquirer's existing shareholders.
Walmart raised its full-year outlook but its stock was down midmorning. Why can that happen?
Expectations were already higher than the new guidance
Guidance raises always lower the price
Prices reflect expectations, so a raise that falls short of what investors hoped for can still disappoint.

terms: About $1.25B in cash, subject to customary purchase-price adjustments
Potential earnout based on Murphy's cumulative three-year performance after closing
Murphy is a mechanical contractor serving mission-critical end markets
DEALS.what: Infrastructure contractor MasTec agreed to buy Murphy Corporation, a mechanical contractor serving mission-critical end markets, for about $1.25 billion in cash, announced November 20. Sellers can earn more through an earnout tied to Murphy's performance over the three years after closing.
DEALS.why: MasTec expands its U.S. mechanical contracting work into mission-critical projects. The earnout shares risk: part of the price is only paid if Murphy keeps performing.
DEALS.say: "An earnout bridges a valuation gap: the seller thinks the business is worth more, the buyer isn't sure, so part of the price depends on future results."
q: Part of MasTec's price for Murphy depends on Murphy's results after closing. What is that called?
An earnout
A breakup fee
A tender offer
A collar
An earnout pays the seller more later if the business hits agreed performance targets.

terms: 31% premium to the 60-day VWAP ending Nov 16
TPG takes a majority stake; Corpay a minority stake
Largest holder Starboard Value and CEO René Lacerte agreed to vote for it
Expected to close in the first half of 2027
DEALS.what: Accounts-payable software company BILL Holdings agreed to be taken private by TPG, partnering with payments company Corpay, for $63.25 a share in cash, valuing BILL at about $6.0 billion. The price is a 31% premium to BILL's 60-day volume-weighted average price before talks leaked. Founder René Lacerte stays CEO.
DEALS.why: BILL's stock had fallen far from its highs, so a private-equity buyer could pay a premium and still buy in cheaply. Corpay gets a strategic stake in a business-payments platform. TPG and Corpay used the same playbook to buy AvidXchange in 2025.
DEALS.say: "It's a take-private: TPG pays a 31% premium in cash for a fallen software stock, with Corpay as a strategic partner, betting the business is worth more out of public markets."
q: BILL's 31% premium is measured against its 60-day VWAP. Why use an average price instead of the last close?
It strips out the jump from leaked deal talks
It makes the premium look smaller
Regulators require it
It includes BILL's debt
Shares often jump once talks leak; an average from before the leak shows the real premium over the undisturbed price.

terms: $3.68B price, subject to cash, debt and working-capital adjustments
Intuit reinvests about $368M (about 10%) into new Bending Spoons shares
No financing condition; regulatory approvals required
Intuit agrees to a two-year non-compete after closing
DEALS.what: Intuit agreed to sell Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for $3.68 billion, announced Nov 19. About $368 million of the proceeds goes back into newly issued Bending Spoons shares, so Intuit keeps a small stake in the buyer. Closing is expected in early 2027.
DEALS.why: Intuit sheds a non-core unit and keeps some upside; Bending Spoons adds another digital business. Source text is AI-generated, so check figures against the filings.
DEALS.say: "Intuit gets cash now and keeps some upside by rolling about 10% of the price into the buyer's stock, while Bending Spoons gets a scaled product to run more efficiently."
q: Intuit takes about 10% of the Mailchimp price in the buyer's new shares. What is one effect?
Intuit keeps some upside in the buyer
Intuit pays Bending Spoons
No regulatory approval is needed
The price becomes all debt
Taking buyer stock means the seller shares in the buyer's future value.

terms: Expected to close in Q3 of fiscal 2027
Aims to build a platform for securely training and deploying open-weight AI models
DEALS.what: Palo Alto Networks agreed to buy AI startup Applied Compute for $4.5 billion, announced alongside its first-quarter results on November 18. The stated aim is a platform for securely training and deploying open-weight AI models. Reports describe the deal as all-stock, and it is expected to close in the third quarter of fiscal 2027.
DEALS.why: The buyer adds AI model infrastructure to its security platform. Paying in stock preserves cash but dilutes existing holders.
DEALS.say: "Palo Alto is buying AI capability rather than building it, and paying in stock keeps its cash for other uses, but existing shareholders are diluted, so the deal needs to be accretive to growth and justify that dilution."
q: Palo Alto is paying for Applied Compute largely with its own shares. What is a downside of that for existing holders?
Dilution of their ownership
Higher cash interest costs
A required tender offer
Automatic loss of voting rights
Issuing new shares to pay for a deal spreads ownership across more shares, diluting existing holders.

terms: Up to ~$1.125B in regulatory and commercial milestones
Blackstone Life Sciences to pay J&J $750M to fund phase 3
Expected to close before end of 2026
DEALS.what: Johnson & Johnson agreed to buy Ollin Biosciences, a clinical-stage biotech in Austin, Texas, for $2.2 billion upfront plus up to about $1.125 billion in further regulatory and commercial milestones, for a potential total of about $3.3 billion. Ollin's lead drug, OLN324, is an experimental VEGF/Ang2 antibody for wet AMD and DME. The deal is subject to regulatory approvals and is expected to close before the end of 2026.
DEALS.why: J&J adds a late-stage eye-disease drug to its pipeline. The milestone structure means it pays the extra amount only if the drug succeeds.
DEALS.say: "The $2.2B is paid upfront, but about a third of the potential value is milestone-based, so J&J shares the clinical and regulatory risk with Ollin's holders. Blackstone Life Sciences funding phase 3 with $750M also keeps that cost off J&J's balance sheet in exchange for royalties."
q: J&J pays $2.2B upfront plus up to about $1.125B on milestones. What is the milestone part similar to?
Contingent consideration (like an earnout)
A break-up fee
A leveraged recap
A stock split
Payments that depend on future events are contingent consideration, similar to an earnout.

terms: ~75% interest in two AWS joint ventures
DEALS.what: Blackstone Digital Infrastructure Trust agreed to buy about a 75% interest in two Amazon Web Services joint ventures in a deal of about $5 billion. The ventures own 13 newly built data-center buildings on two AWS campuses. AWS keeps about 25% and leases all of the properties. The deal is expected to close in the fourth quarter and is subject to closing conditions.
DEALS.why: The buyer gets long-term rent from a large cloud tenant on stabilized assets. AWS keeps using the campuses without owning all of the real estate.
DEALS.say: "It's a sale-leaseback: AWS turns buildings into cash but keeps using them under a 12-year triple-net lease, and Blackstone's trust earns a 7.0% initial cap rate on stabilized, tenant-backed assets."
q: In a sale-leaseback like Blackstone's AWS data-center deal, what does the seller (AWS) do?
Sells the property and rents it back
Buys the property from its tenant
Spins the property off to shareholders
Raises equity by issuing new shares
A sale-leaseback converts owned real estate into cash while the seller keeps using the property as a tenant.
The deal has a 7.0% initial cap rate. What does a cap rate measure?
Net operating income divided by property price
Debt divided by equity
The premium paid over market price
Annual rent growth
Cap rate is a property's net operating income divided by its price, a quick yield measure for real estate.

DEALS.target: Double Eagle IV and V subsidiaries
terms: About 15.56 million Diamondback shares plus $2.15 billion in cash
Adds about 176,000 net Midland Basin acres
DEALS.what: Diamondback Energy agreed to buy subsidiaries of Double Eagle IV Midco and Double Eagle V Midco for about 15.56 million Diamondback shares plus $2.15 billion in cash, adding about 176,000 net acres in the Permian's Midland Basin. Diamondback says the price is about 4.0 times estimated 2027 EBITDA. The total dollar value depends on Diamondback's share price, so it's listed as cash plus shares.
DEALS.why: Diamondback keeps consolidating the Midland Basin, buying more drilling inventory next to its own acreage. Using part stock lets the sellers share in the combined company.
DEALS.say: "It's Permian consolidation: Diamondback adds about 176,000 acres for roughly 4x next year's EBITDA, paying in cash and stock."
q: Diamondback pays about 4.0x estimated 2027 EBITDA. What does a lower multiple usually signal?
A cheaper price for each dollar of earnings
A bigger cash payment
A higher interest rate
A larger share count
EV/EBITDA compares price to earnings power; a lower multiple means paying less per dollar of EBITDA.

terms: C$11.00 cash or 0.25 Strathcona shares per Greenfire share
DEALS.what: Canadian oil producer Strathcona Resources agreed to buy Alberta oil sands producer Greenfire Resources for about C$2.7 to C$2.9 billion (about $1.91 billion) including debt. Greenfire holders can choose C$11.00 in cash or 0.25 Strathcona shares per share. The deal is expected to close in early 2027.
DEALS.why: Strathcona is expanding in Alberta's oil sands by combining two producers in the same region. Waterous Energy Fund owns about 72% of Greenfire and 57% of Strathcona and supports the deal.
DEALS.say: "Because Waterous owns most of both companies, this is a related-party deal, so the cash-or-stock election and the roughly 39% cash premium matter for how minority shareholders are treated."
q: Greenfire holders can pick C$11.00 cash or 0.25 Strathcona shares. What is this called?
A tender offer only
A cash-or-stock election
A leveraged buyout
A spin-off
The target's shareholders choose between cash and buyer shares, which is a cash-or-stock election.
Waterous owns about 72% of Greenfire and 57% of Strathcona. Why does that matter?
It makes the deal tax free
It is a related-party deal with a common controlling holder
It blocks any premium
It means no approval is needed
One holder sits on both sides, so minority shareholder protections matter.

terms: 0.7463 Hancock Whitney shares per Trustmark share
DEALS.what: Hancock Whitney agreed to buy fellow Gulf South regional bank Trustmark in an all-stock deal valued at about $3.2 billion. Trustmark shareholders will receive 0.7463 Hancock Whitney shares for each share they own.
DEALS.why: Regional banks are merging to gain scale and cut costs. Hancock Whitney expects the deal to add about 7% to its 2028 earnings per share.
DEALS.say: "Because it's all stock at a fixed 0.7463 ratio, Trustmark holders share in Hancock Whitney's stock moves until closing, and the buyer is betting cost savings make it about 7% accretive by 2028."
q: Hancock Whitney says the deal is about 7% accretive to 2028 EPS. What does that mean?
Its EPS should be about 7% lower
Its EPS should be about 7% higher
Its stock will rise 7%
It pays a 7% premium
Accretive means the buyer's earnings per share rise because of the deal.
Trustmark holders get a fixed 0.7463 Hancock Whitney shares each. If Hancock Whitney's stock falls before closing, what happens?
Their payout keeps the same dollar value
Their payout loses value
They get extra cash
The deal is canceled
With a fixed exchange ratio, the payout's value moves with the buyer's stock price.

terms: MM Group expects about €1.8–1.9 billion in proceeds
Expected to close in the first half of 2027
DEALS.what: Private equity firm KPS Capital Partners agreed to buy 70% of MM Packaging, the folding-carton business of Austria's Mayr-Melnhof (MM Group), at a €2.4 billion enterprise value. MM Group keeps 30% and expects about €1.8–1.9 billion in proceeds. MM shares rose about 9% the next day.
DEALS.why: MM Group focuses on its board business and gets cash; KPS carves out a standalone global packaging company. Keeping 30% lets the seller share in any upside.
DEALS.say: "It's a carve-out: the seller keeps a 30% stake, so the headline €2.4B enterprise value is more than the cash it actually receives."
q: MM Group sells 70% at a €2.4B enterprise value but expects only ~€1.8–1.9B in proceeds. Why is the cash lower?
It keeps a 30% stake and EV includes more than equity cash
KPS paid in stock
Taxes are deducted first
The deal was cancelled
Enterprise value covers the whole business; the seller only gets cash for the part it sells.

DEALS.what: Marvell agreed to buy Lumentum, a maker of lasers and optical parts for AI data centers, in an all-stock deal valued at about $115 billion, or about $1,132 per Lumentum share at Oct 28 prices. Marvell owners would hold about 67% of the combined company and Lumentum owners about 33%, with closing expected in the first half of 2028.
DEALS.why: Marvell makes chips that move data, and it wants more optical technology and factory capacity as AI data centers shift from copper to light. The companies expect more than $1 billion of yearly cost savings and say the deal should add to Marvell's adjusted EPS in the first year after closing.
DEALS.say: "Because Marvell is paying a fixed 4.5 shares, the $115 billion headline moves with its stock, so Lumentum's owners take on Marvell's share price risk until closing in 2028."
q: Marvell is paying a fixed 4.5 Marvell shares for each Lumentum share. If Marvell's stock falls before closing, what happens to Lumentum owners' payout?
It stays locked at the $1,132 headline price
It rises because Marvell issues extra shares
Its value falls because the 4.5 ratio is fixed
It converts into cash at the Oct 28 stock price
With a fixed exchange ratio, the share count stays the same, so the dollar value moves up and down with the buyer's stock.
Marvell must pay Lumentum $3.2 billion if the merger ends over certain regulatory problems. Why would Lumentum ask for this fee?
It pays Lumentum for failed-review risk
It lets Marvell skip the U.S. antitrust review
It raises the exchange ratio when deals close
It funds the $1 billion of planned cost savings
A reverse termination fee protects the target, which can lose years and business momentum if regulators block the merger.

DEALS.what: Kansas City-based UMB Financial agreed to buy El Dorado Savings Bank, a California bank with about $2.4 billion of assets, for about $506 million in cash and stock. Closing is expected in the first quarter of 2027 if regulators and El Dorado's owners approve.
DEALS.why: El Dorado brings $2.1 billion of deposits and 35 branches in California and Nevada, taking UMB to 227 branches in 15 states. UMB gets a much bigger West Coast footprint and a cheap, steady base of deposits to fund loans.
DEALS.say: "UMB is paying about $506 million, mostly for El Dorado's $2.1 billion of deposits and 35 West Coast branches, which give it cheap funding and a bigger footprint in California."
q: UMB Financial is paying for El Dorado Savings Bank with about 52% cash and 48% UMB stock. What does the stock part mean for El Dorado's owners?
They must sell their shares back to El Dorado for cash
They become part-owners of UMB and share in its results
They receive UMB bonds that pay a fixed yearly interest rate
They keep their El Dorado shares, which stay publicly listed
Sellers paid in stock swap their shares for the buyer's shares, so they own part of the combined bank and share its future ups and downs.
UMB Financial's ~$506M purchase of El Dorado Savings Bank adds $2.1 billion of deposits and 35 branches. Why do banks often buy other banks for their deposits?
Deposits count as revenue the day the deal closes
Regulators require banks to double deposits every five years
Deposits let a bank skip its own capital requirements
Deposits are a cheap, steady source of money to fund loans
Banks earn money by lending, and customer deposits usually cost much less than borrowing in the bond market, so a big deposit base is valuable.

DEALS.what: French industrial giant Schneider Electric agreed to buy PTC, a U.S. maker of design and engineering software, for $205 a share in cash.
DEALS.why: Schneider sells equipment for factories and buildings. Owning PTC's software adds recurring revenue and ties its hardware to the tools engineers use every day.
DEALS.say: "It's a strategic deal: a hardware company paying up for recurring software revenue it can cross-sell to its industrial customers."
q: Schneider is best described as what kind of buyer?
Financial buyer
Strategic buyer
Activist
Sovereign fund
It's an operating company buying a business that fits its own, so it can pay for synergies.
Paying all cash means PTC shareholders:
Become Schneider shareholders
Receive cash and exit
Keep their PTC shares
Get bonds
In an all-cash deal, target shareholders are paid out and no longer own the business.

DEALS.what: DoorDash agreed to buy Instacart's parent company, Maplebear, for $65 a share, about $17 billion of equity value. Instacart holders can choose cash, DoorDash stock or a mix, but stock is capped at 25% of the total, and the deal should close by late 2027 or the first half of 2028.
DEALS.why: DoorDash gets the leading U.S. grocery-delivery platform and its retailer software, plus a bigger ad business. Together they can offer local grocers one delivery network to compete with Walmart and Amazon.
DEALS.say: "It's a mostly-cash strategic deal funded with a bridge loan, so the key risks are antitrust review and how much new debt DoorDash takes on while trying to keep its investment-grade rating."
q: DoorDash is paying for Instacart with at least 75% cash and at most 25% DoorDash stock. What is the main benefit of the stock portion for DoorDash?
It uses less new debt and protects the credit rating
It guarantees antitrust approval from regulators
It lets DoorDash skip the shareholder vote
It locks in a lower price per Instacart share
Paying part of the price in stock means borrowing less, which helps DoorDash keep its investment-grade rating.
JPMorgan gave DoorDash a 364-day bridge loan commitment for the Instacart deal. What is a bridge loan used for?
Paying Instacart's employee retention bonuses
Covering the breakup fee if the deal fails
Short-term funding until bonds are issued later
Buying back DoorDash shares after closing
A bridge loan guarantees the cash is there at signing; the buyer usually replaces it with longer-term bonds before or at closing.

DEALS.what: Private equity firm EQT agreed to take diagnostics company Qiagen private for €46.50 a share in cash. Including about $1.1 billion of debt, the deal is worth about €10.8 billion (~$12.1 billion).
DEALS.why: Qiagen says private ownership will let it invest for the long term and move faster. Analysts at William Blair put the price at about 15x expected 2027 EBITDA, below similar life-science deals.
DEALS.say: "This is a take-private: EQT pays a ~40% premium over the undisturbed price, measured before takeover rumors leaked in July."
q: The ~40% premium is measured against Qiagen's price before takeover reports in July. Why use that date?
It was the highest price of the year
It is the undisturbed price, before rumors pushed the stock up
Regulators require July prices
It is the date the deal closes
Rumors lift a stock, so premiums are measured from the undisturbed price.

DEALS.what: EQT Corp., the largest U.S. natural gas producer, agreed to buy rival Range Resources by swapping its own shares for Range's. Reuters put Range's equity value at about $12.8 billion, and the combined company is worth more than $50 billion including debt.
DEALS.why: Data centers are driving up demand for natural gas, and a bigger producer can drill more cheaply and sell gas more effectively. EQT expects about $325 million a year in savings within two years, rising to over $600 million long term.
DEALS.say: "It's an all-stock merger of equals in spirit: Range holders take a ~20% premium in EQT shares and end up owning about 27% of the combined gas giant."
q: Range holders get 0.987 EQT shares each. If EQT stock falls 10% before closing, what happens to the value Range holders receive?
It stays fixed at $54.91
It falls too, because the share ratio is fixed
It rises
The deal is cancelled automatically
With a fixed exchange ratio, the target's payout moves with the buyer's stock price.
Why might EQT's stock fall when the deal is announced while Range's jumps?
EQT is paying a premium and issuing new shares, diluting its holders
Range is paying EQT
All-stock deals are illegal
EQT is going private
The buyer pays a premium and issues shares, so its stock often dips while the target rises toward the offer.

terms: Part paid only if milestones are hit
DEALS.what: Swiss drugmaker Ferring, a big name in fertility treatments, signed a deal to buy Gameto, a private biotech that uses cell engineering to develop treatments for infertility and other women's reproductive health issues. The deal is worth up to about $1.38 billion, but part of that is only paid if Gameto hits development, regulatory and sales goals.
DEALS.why: Ferring gets a pipeline of new fertility technology, including an egg-maturation program that is still investigational in the U.S., and can use its global sales network to reach more patients. Tying much of the price to milestones protects Ferring if the science or FDA approval doesn't pan out.
DEALS.say: "Ferring's up-to-$1.38 billion deal for Gameto ties part of the price to future milestones, which is how buyers handle the risk that an unapproved biotech product never makes it to market."
q: Ferring's deal for Gameto is worth 'up to' $1.38B because some payments depend on future milestones. What is that kind of payment called?
Contingent consideration paid later if goals are met
A breakup fee paid if the deal fails to close
A tender offer made directly to public shareholders
A dividend recap funded by new debt at the target
Milestone payments are contingent consideration: the buyer pays more only if the target reaches set goals.
Gameto's main program is not yet FDA approved. Why does that make milestone payments attractive to Ferring when buying Gameto?
They let Ferring avoid any regulatory review of the deal
They make Gameto's shareholders pay Ferring's legal fees
They cut what Ferring pays if the product never gets approved
They guarantee Ferring a fixed return on the whole purchase
Paying part of the price only on success shifts the risk of a failed trial or rejection back to the sellers.

terms: Paid with committed financing and existing resources
DEALS.what: Ahold Delhaize, the Dutch owner of Food Lion, Stop & Shop and Albert, agreed to buy Tesco's grocery business in Czechia and Slovakia for an enterprise value of about €1.2 billion. The unit has more than 360 company-run stores plus 100+ franchise stores and about €3.5 billion in sales.
DEALS.why: Combined with its Albert stores, Ahold expects to become the top grocery brand in Czechia and gains a first foothold in Slovakia. Grocery is a scale game, so more stores mean better buying power with suppliers and lower costs per store.
DEALS.say: "Ahold Delhaize is paying about 7.2 times EBITDA for Tesco's Czech and Slovak stores, but closer to 5 times once you count synergies, which is how a buyer can justify a price that looks higher than it feels."
q: Ahold Delhaize says its Tesco Czechia and Slovakia purchase costs about 7.2x EBITDA, or 5.0x 'including synergies.' Why is the second multiple lower?
Synergies are added to EBITDA, making the denominator larger
Synergies cut the purchase price Ahold Delhaize pays Tesco at closing
The lower multiple leaves out the leases that Tesco's stores carry
The lower multiple uses Tesco's sales instead of EBITDA as its base
Adding expected cost savings to the target's EBITDA makes the denominator bigger, so the price looks cheaper as a multiple.
Ahold Delhaize gives Tesco Czechia and Slovakia two values: ~€1.2B EV and ~€1.7B 'lease-adjusted' EV. What explains the gap?
The €0.5B gap is a breakup fee owed if regulators block the deal
The €0.5B gap is the extra amount Ahold expects to save each year
The €0.5B gap counts store lease obligations as a form of debt
The €0.5B gap is the value of Tesco's franchise stores in Slovakia
Under IFRS 16, store leases are treated like debt, so adding them raises enterprise value; the matching EBITDA is also measured before rent.

DEALS.what: Affle, an Indian mobile ad-tech company, agreed to buy Nasdaq-listed Perion for $11.70 per share in cash, valuing Perion's equity at about $420 million. Perion's board backed the deal, which still needs shareholder and U.S. antitrust approval.
DEALS.why: Affle adds Perion's retail media, connected-TV and digital billboard ad tools to its mobile marketing platform, hoping to sell more to the same advertisers. Perion keeps its brand, and its shareholders get a certain cash price.
DEALS.say: "Affle's all-cash offer for Perion pays a 34.5% premium and includes a 40-day go-shop, which lets Perion's board test the market for a better bid before the deal closes."
src: Perion press release via Yahoo Finance
q: Affle's deal to buy Perion includes a 40-day 'go-shop' period. What does that allow Perion to do?
Ask Affle to raise its $11.70 price once each week
Actively seek competing offers from other buyers
Let Perion holders swap shares for Affle stock
Delay its shareholder vote until regulators approve
A go-shop lets the target solicit rival bids for a set time after signing, helping the board show it got the best price.
Affle is paying $11.70 per share for Perion, a 34.5% premium to its Oct 30 close. Roughly where did Perion stock close that day?
About $8.70, or $11.70 divided by 1.345
About $7.66, or $11.70 minus 34.5% of it
About $15.74, or $11.70 times 1.345
Premium = offer / prior price - 1, so the prior price is $11.70 / 1.345, about $8.70.
